name: Gin Rummy
intro: Learn Gin Rummy from scratch: drawing and discarding, sets and runs, deadwood, knocking, gin and laying off, then the strategy that wins more hands.

units.name: How Gin Rummy works
units.blurb: Drawing and discarding, melds, deadwood, knocking, gin and laying off.

lessons.title: Gin Rummy: the deal and a turn
lessons.summary: Gin Rummy is a two-player card game. Each player gets 10 cards; on your turn you draw one and discard one. Learn how a turn works.
lessons.wrap: Draw one, discard one. Next: melds.

steps.text:
Gin Rummy is played by two players with one deck. Each player gets 10 cards; the rest form the stock, and one card is turned up to start the discard pile.

On your turn you draw one card, either the top of the stock or the top of the discard pile, then discard one card face up.
Quick check.
steps.prompt: How many cards do you hold between turns?
steps.explain: Ten. You hold 11 for a moment after drawing, then discard back to 10.

lessons.title: Melds: sets and runs
lessons.summary: A meld is a set of three or four cards of the same rank, or a run of three or more in the same suit. Learn to spot both in your hand.
lessons.wrap: Sets and runs are melds. Next: deadwood.

steps.text:
You want to arrange your cards into melds:

  • a set: three or four cards of the same rank, like three 7s;
  • a run: three or more cards in a row in the same suit, like 4, 5, 6 of hearts. Aces are low: A, 2, 3 is a run, but Q, K, A isn’t.
Find the set.
steps.prompt: Tap the three cards that make a set.
steps.wrong: A set is three cards of the same rank.

steps.text: There are two runs in this hand. One is in hearts.
steps.prompt: Tap the cards of the other run.
steps.wrong: A run is three or more cards in a row, all the same suit.

lessons.title: Deadwood
lessons.summary: Cards that aren’t in a meld are deadwood, counted in points: aces 1, number cards their value, face cards 10. Learn to count it.
lessons.wrap: Less deadwood is better. Next: what to discard.

steps.text:
Any card that isn’t part of a meld is deadwood. Deadwood is counted in points: aces 1, number cards their number, and jacks, queens and kings 10 each.

This hand has three melds and one king left over: 10 points of deadwood.
This hand has no melds at all.
steps.prompt: Which cards add the most deadwood?
steps.explain: The king and queen: 10 points each. High cards are expensive deadwood.

lessons.title: Choosing a discard
lessons.summary: After drawing, discard the card that leaves you the least deadwood. Practise with real hands, and learn why high loose cards go first.
lessons.wrap: Discard the card that leaves you the least deadwood.

steps.text: You’ve drawn the 2 of spades. You have 11 cards; discard one.
steps.prompt: Discard the card that leaves the least deadwood.
steps.wrong: That leaves more deadwood than you need. Which loose card is worth the most?

steps.text: You have a set of queens and a run of clubs.
steps.prompt: Discard the card that leaves the least deadwood.
steps.wrong: Keep your melds together and throw your most expensive loose card.

lessons.title: Knocking, gin and laying off
lessons.summary: Knock when your deadwood is 10 or less, or go gin with none. Learn how a hand ends, how it’s scored and how laying off works.
lessons.wrap: You know every rule. Test yourself in the rules check.

steps.text:
When your deadwood is 10 or less after discarding, you may knock to end the hand. Both players show their melds, and the other player may lay off: add their loose cards to your melds (a fourth 7 on your three 7s, the 7 of hearts on your 4-5-6).

You score the difference in deadwood. But if the other player ends up with deadwood equal to or less than yours, they undercut you and score the difference plus 25.
With no deadwood at all you go gin: 25 bonus points plus your opponent’s deadwood, and they can’t lay off.
steps.wrong: Find the one card that isn’t part of a meld.
steps.done: Gin! Every card is in a meld.

steps.text: You knocked with three 7s and the 4-5-6 of hearts showing.
steps.prompt: Which of your opponent’s loose cards can they lay off?
steps.explain: The 7 of hearts extends your run of hearts (it could also be the fourth 7). The 9 of spades fits nothing.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Five questions on the rules. Pass to unlock the strategy.

lessons.title: Gin Rummy rules check
lessons.summary: Test your Gin Rummy rules: melds, deadwood, discarding, knocking, gin, laying off and the undercut.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the strategy.

steps.text: Question 1.
steps.prompt: Tap the cards of the run.
steps.wrong: A run is three in a row in one suit. Aces are low.

steps.text: Question 2.
steps.prompt: How much is a jack worth as deadwood?

steps.text: Question 3.
steps.prompt: Discard the card that leaves the least deadwood.
steps.wrong: Keep the melds; drop the loose card worth the most.

steps.text: Question 4.
options: When your deadwood is 10 or less

steps.text: Question 5.
steps.prompt: You knock with 6 deadwood; after laying off, your opponent has 4. What happens?
steps.explain: An undercut: they score the difference plus 25.

units.name: Strategy
units.blurb: Dump high cards, read the discards, and know when to knock.

lessons.title: Get rid of high cards early
lessons.summary: High loose cards are expensive if your opponent knocks. Learn why discarding kings and queens early usually beats waiting for a meld.
lessons.wrap: Early on, throw loose high cards; keep low cards and near-melds.

steps.text:
Your opponent could knock at any time. If they do, every loose king or queen in your hand costs you 10 points.

So early in the hand, discard high cards that aren’t close to a meld. Keep low cards and near-melds (pairs like 4♣ 4♦, or 8♥ 9♥) that one more card would complete.
No melds yet.
steps.prompt: Discard a card a good player would throw first.
steps.wrong: Keep your pairs and connected cards. Throw a high card that’s on its own.

lessons.title: Watch what your opponent picks up
lessons.summary: Cards your opponent takes from the discard pile tell you what they’re collecting. Learn to avoid feeding their melds.
lessons.wrap: Don’t discard what your opponent is collecting.

steps.text: Your opponent just picked up the 8 of spades from the discard pile, instead of drawing from the stock. They must want it for a meld.
steps.explain: The 9 of spades sits right next to the 8 they took and could complete a run of spades for them. The jack of diamonds is nowhere near it.

steps.text: Cards your opponent throws away tell you what they don’t want.
steps.prompt: They just discarded the 6 of diamonds. Is the 6 of clubs fairly safe for you to discard?
steps.explain: Fairly safe: if they were collecting 6s, they wouldn’t have thrown one away.

lessons.title: Knock early or wait for gin?
lessons.summary: Knocking early wins many small hands; waiting for gin risks an undercut and a big loss. Learn when each makes sense.
lessons.wrap: Knock early and often; go for gin only when it’s close and safe.

steps.text: You can knock with 10 deadwood (the king). It’s early in the hand.
steps.prompt: What do strong players usually do?
steps.explain: Knock. Early in the hand your opponent probably has lots of deadwood, so you score well and they have little time to improve.

steps.text: Late in the hand you have 9 deadwood, and your opponent has been picking up cards and discarding low ones.
steps.prompt: What’s the risk of knocking now?
options: They may have very little deadwood and undercut you
steps.explain: An undercut. Late in the hand, a low knock is safer, or wait for gin.
